title_en: 'It Was Somewhere Between Location Scouting and Espionage' — Gangland Tales From the Frontline of Rockstar’s Real-Life Grand Theft Auto Research
summary_en: A former Rockstar developer tells stories about the real-life research that went into making the Grand Theft Auto games so authentic.
body_en:
Gregory Johnson was sitting in the back of a police car, but he wasn’t under arrest. In fact, the cops were just as nervous as him. Johnson, an experienced researcher for Rockstar, was scouting the underbelly of Los Angeles for Grand Theft Auto 5, an open-world crime game set in a fictionalized L.A. called Los Santos, which is Spanish for “The Saints.” Outside the car window, there were no saints to be found.
“We were doing a ride along in East L.A., very late at night,” Johnson told IGN in a recent interview. “It's still an active gang neighborhood where stuff is going down, so I'm knowing all the signs and seeing a lot of it, and I was super nervous about it. I was like, ‘We're probably okay, but what if we're not?’”
As the car pulled a corner, a whistle cried out from a nearby rooftop. Another series of whistles quickly followed, fading as they moved along a human daisy chain — an alarm system from a series of rooftop sentries to warn other gang members cops were on the prowl. With that, a couple of bikes shot down alleyways, pedalling fast to catch up before pulling up either side of the car to escort it on its patrol through the neighbourhood. The riders stared into the windows through masks.
“The Mexican gangs of Los Angeles are known to be very organized,” Johnson explained. “And I quickly got to the point where I was like, I know we've got police with us. I know they're armed. The logic of the moment holds that nobody wants this to turn into any situation. They don't want to generally initiate violence with the police. We don't want violence. We're just here to get a feel for the place and maybe poke our long lenses out of the windows and shoot some pictures.
“So we just got through it and ran our routes, and got everybody back to the hotel safely, but once I saw the neighborhood activate… I mean, it's amazing to see if you're going to try and duplicate it with the gameplay, right? But when you're actually in it, you're like, ‘This could go bad.’”
Even that feeling is important — the dread, the worry that things could boil over at any moment — when trying to capture the essence of a city, from its decadent hilltop houses in the Hollywood Hills to its low-income neighbourhoods over the Los Angeles River. Mood is a hard thing to capture unless you’ve felt the electricity in the air yourself as fight or flight kicks in and the hairs on the back of your neck stand to attention.
“I had to keep everybody cool in the group,” Johnson, a Floridian who lived most of his life in New York, remembered. “We've got a bunch of guys from Scotland and England, Ireland. Never seen anything like it. They're like, ‘Is everything okay, Greg?’ ‘Yeah, everything's fine.’ Completely lying. ‘Everything's fine, guys.’ It was somewhere between location scouting and espionage.”
Johnson himself knew the streets fairly well already, but he was partly recruited not just because of what he knew, but because of who he knew. Having worked on hip-hop’s Vibe Magazine for 16 years, as well as other prestigious music mags like Source, he was already embedded in the culture. He knew the people in the music industry Rockstar was working with, and helped make introductions where he could. He had his finger pushed hard into the pulse of an ever-shifting culture.
“Dan Houser had a vision for a professional research team that could easily deliver academic information,” Johnson explained. “Basically an internal form of reporting, cultural research. The role grew right as we established the department, but he had tried to get together various versions of it, and when he hired me and a couple other people around that time, I had an academic background as well as a background in hip hop journalism, and I knew the culture inside and out. We would go through tons of pop culture and various applicable subcultures.
“Rockstar has represented Jamaican yardies extremely well. The mafia culture in GTA, the Yakuza culture in GTA — all of these different subcultures and themes were really rich targets for deep dives. The better the graphics got, the better the gameplay got, the better the voiceovers got — the ambient stuff, the missions — the more background information was required to distill it into these memorable, immersive gameplay experiences. We did real life research, and these broad surveys of popular culture and the popular imagination, depending on the setting of the game, the timing of the game, and the artistic and creative direction.”
At one point, a smuggler came across Rockstar’s radar. This was a guy who knew the late drug lord Pablo Escobar personally and was a major player in the Cocaine Cowboys era, the Scarface days, when the Medellin Cartel trafficked white powder into Miami through the ‘70s and ‘80s. According to Johnson, some of the interviews with the smuggler likely informed the Cayo Perico heist in GTA Online.
“This was one of the guys that helped the Colombians figure out their underwater submersible system, where they were, with submarines of various quality, able to bring stuff from the Colombian coast into the U.S.,” Johnson said. “That later changed. The Colombian cartels ended up cutting a deal with the Mexican cartels. But this guy was from the era when they were still getting it into the United States directly.”
The drug runner told Rockstar stories about having to pay tribute to Pablo Escobar, and the time he got kidnapped by another cartel member and held in a dingy room god-knows-where, wondering if he would be killed. His stories gave the research team a peek behind the curtain of organized crime arguably at its height. But even talking to him — despite strict NDAs protecting identities — came with its own concerns.
“Just hanging out with this guy and his sidekick in Miami, it occurred to me that revenge could visit him at any moment,” Johnson said with a nervous laugh. “And they're not going to distinguish.”
Some of the most intense encounters weren’t one-off meetings — they were in the studio where Rockstar recorded its motion capture and voice lines. Radio DJ turned writer Lazlow, Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser, and director of production Rod Edge were exposed to these the most as they ensured words on the script survived the transition to audio files.
“DJ Poo and Estevan Oriol and Mister Cartoon were bringing real gangsters,” Johnson explained. “Some of these guys are famous for bringing these guys in for bit parts and minor roles in some of the L.A. street films. It's like the Sopranos where Tony Sirico is a former Gambino associate, and he ended up getting a recurring role as Paulie Walnuts. Or The Wire, which was another television program that was a huge influence on me and Rockstar, to varying degrees. The Wire was known for bringing people out of the Baltimore streets and giving them roles on the show — ‘Snoop’ Pearson, Nathan Barksdale, and a few other legit Baltimore gangsters.
“So we would do a lot of that stuff. Some of these guys are like Salvadorian gangsters with a face full of tattoos, and you're like, ‘Say this line again with more enthusiasm.’ Or they'll tell you, ‘Check this out, bro. We wouldn't say that like that. We say this like this.’ So even though we would try to do a ton of research and make the scripts as authentic as possible, somebody that's lived that life is going to have the most current, up to date jargon and slang and lingo. A lot of them were just super excited to have their horizons opened, and get an opportunity to do voiceover work.”
It wasn’t all fear, either. When Johnson worked on GTA 6 , the research team took a helicopter from Miami to Key West, flying low over the barrier islands with a long lens — Johnson never imagined he’d see the city and its surrounding areas like this. Sometimes up-close, sometimes a bird’s-eye view, always documenting and capturing the vibe to bottle up and digitize, top to bottom, micro and macro — this authenticity and obsessive attention to detail is what makes Rockstar open-worlds feel so alive.
“There was a ton of stuff,” Johnson said. “I would visit the prisons. They were nervous but hilarious. It was our job to give the developers the exposure they needed to any one of these areas of the game, whether it was the underworld stuff or street racers, or whatever. Anything we could do to make the experience more immersive and authentic, like sitting down with FBI agents or gangsters or working as location scouts. Basically we had a broad mandate, and I think we did a pretty good job of it.”
The extreme lengths Rockstar developers go to in the aim of creating authentic worldsare partly why there’s such a buzz behind GTA 6, which has already generated $1 billion in preorder sales . No one does it like Rockstar, and the audience knows this.
Rockstar recently spoke about its GTA 6 research trips (some of which Johnson attended — he left the company halfway through development). It’s where every game starts, but the process continues throughout development to keep the writers and designers keyed into the culture of the place they’re basing the game world on. The company even built out an entire studio just to write dialogue for pedestrian NPCs, such is its commitment to the craft of making a living simulation.
GTA 6 launches on November 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S.
